cells.tense: You're in the middle of it, adjusting as you go, and the adjusting is working.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you keep fine-tuning and leave it alone for a day, then note what changed without your hand on it.
cells.core:
You don't have to force the direction right now. Feeling and intention are pulling the same way, and you can tell without checking. The small calibrations you're making — adding this, letting that go, shifting the blend — are the actual work, and they're landing where they need to. That's what this alignment feels like from the inside: not still, just unforced.

What it sets up is more of the same, on purpose. If you leave one thing alone for a day, unadjusted, you'll find out whether you were carrying it or it was carrying you. Either way you'll know something you can use about what's actually yours to steer and what runs fine when you step back.
cells.sheetLine: Feeling and direction are on the same line — and you can tell without checking.
cells.verb: finding the natural rhythm of what moves you and letting your direction and your feeling land on the same line
cells.place: the active calibration that keeps a flow going, sensing what to add and what to take out as it moves

cells.tense: You're leaning into a version of this that hasn't arrived, adjusting for a moment you can't see yet.
cells.ask: Write down every adjustment you're holding, then cross out everything that isn't due today — do only what's left on the page.
cells.core:
You're adjusting for things that haven't happened. Before anyone asks, before the moment arrives, you've already shifted to meet it — and all that tuning is coming out of today. The momentum you actually have gets spent on versions of the road you can't drive from where you sit. That's the cost: the tuning is real but it's landing on nothing yet.

The list you're carrying is mostly predictions. Put all of it on paper, mark the one or two items due today, and let the rest wait until they're actually in front of you. The pace you get back is the pace that was yours to begin with. Nothing on that page stops being true because you wrote it down instead of holding it.

cells.tense: The adjusting has stopped, and part of you is still standing where it stopped.
cells.ask: Do the smallest piece of one thing you've been circling, for the length of a cup of tea, and stop when the tea's done.
cells.core:
Feeling used to move you, and it doesn't right now. Something you stopped adjusting for is sitting there, and you've left it — not finished it, not put it down, just left it. Starting again looks bigger than it is from where you're standing. The gap is smaller than it appears, and it's still there for you to cross.

You don't have to restart the whole engine. Pick the smallest visible piece of one thing, give it ten minutes, and stop when the ten are up. That's not a fix. It's a test of whether the current still runs, and you'll learn something either way. If nothing moves, that's information about the state of things, not a verdict on you.

cells.tense: You're constantly recalibrating and not counting it as anything you're doing.
cells.ask: At the end of today, write down one adjustment you made that held things together, and name it as yours.
cells.core:
You do the work — shift the timing of a conversation, soften a plan, add something here and take it out there — and the flow holds because you keep touching it. But you describe it as if the days were arranging themselves. The calibration is real, it's yours, and it doesn't make it into the account of what you did.

One line at the end of today changes that. Not a journal. One note: the adjustment you made, and the fact that you made it. You don't have to announce it or turn it into a project. It's a record, for you, of something running under your own radar. What gets named can be built on. What stays nameless keeps running anyway, just without hands on it.
